In this murky realm lived Ayana, a weaver whose fingers moved with impossible grace. She grew weary of the colorless world and decided to create something new. From the mist itself, she spun silver threads. From the distant stars, she pulled down golden light. From the dreams of sleeping creatures, she gathered crimson and violet hues.

The tapestry became the sun, rising for the first time. But Ayana understood that eternal light would be as wearisome as eternal twilight. So each evening, she gently folds her tapestry away, letting darkness rest upon the world. Each morning, she unfurls it again.

And so the first dawn broke, and every dawn since. They say if you watch the sunrise carefully, you can still see Ayana's fingers in the threading rays of light, weaving the day anew.

One day, the Earth spoke: "Great Sun, your light is magnificent, but it is also relentless. Grant us rest."

The Sun, in her pride, refused. "Without my light, you would have nothing."

That night, the Moon appeared—a gift from the stars. Gentle and silver, she did not compete with the Sun but complemented her. When the Moon rose, she created something the Sun never could: shadows.

The first shadow fell beneath a mountain, and in that darkness, life discovered secrets—cool refuge, quiet dreams, and the beauty of mystery. Animals learned to rest. Flowers closed their petals. The world breathed.

When the Sun returned at dawn, she saw that the shadows had made her light more precious. She learned that true radiance comes not from illuminating everything, but from knowing when to step back.

From that day forward, Sun and Moon shared the sky, teaching all beings that both light and shadow are necessary for balance.
